PART SIX
Health & Body
CHAPTER 52
When You Are Ill
An ordinary task now needs planning. You consider whether
you have enough energy to shower, answer a message, or make
something to eat. People ask how you are, and the answer
depends on whether they mean the symptoms, the treatment, or
what it is like to live around both.
Illness may have interrupted a few days or altered the shape of
your life. You might be impatient to recover, frightened by
uncertainty, or tired of explaining a condition others cannot see.
Receiving care can itself feel unfamiliar if you are usually the
person who provides it.
Your needs deserve attention while you are ill. You can ask God
for healing and tell Him about the smaller difficulties: the
uncomfortable night, a canceled plan, or the effort of another
appointment.
A woman tells Jesus the whole truth
Mark 5:25–34
A woman who had been bleeding for twelve years heard about
Jesus. She had suffered under many physicians, spent all she
had, and grown worse. Coming through the crowd behind Him,

258
she touched His clothing, believing that she would be healed.
The bleeding stopped.
Jesus turned and asked who had touched Him. His disciples
pointed to the crowd pressing around them, but He continued
looking. The woman came forward trembling, fell before Him,
and told Him the whole truth. He called her daughter, spoke of
her faith, and sent her away in peace, free of her affliction.
Mark records a healing and a personal encounter. The woman's
long history of illness was heard in the middle of a crowded day.
Jesus addressed her as someone who belonged, after she had
come forward afraid.
This account gives Christians reason to ask Him for healing. Her
outcome cannot be used to decide how much faith another
patient has, and the account of unsuccessful treatment gives no
instruction to abandon medical care.
You may recognize the effort of telling your history again.
Where you can, tell someone more than the medical summary.
What part of being ill is hardest to live with today? Is there
something people assume you can manage that you currently
cannot?
Ask the church to come near
James 5:13–16 invites a sick person to call the church's elders to
pray and anoint them in the Lord's name. Prayer is an active
responsibility within the Christian community. You can ask for
it even when you feel too tired or uncertain to lead the
conversation yourself.
The passage speaks confidently about God's response. Read it
alongside the New Testament's accounts of believers who
continued to experience illness. Paul refers to Timothy's
frequent ailments in 1 Timothy 5:23 and says in 2 Timothy 4:20
that he left Trophimus sick at Miletus. Continued sickness does
not establish that someone failed to pray faithfully.

259
Ask for prayer in a form you can receive. Perhaps you would
welcome a short visit, a call, or someone quietly praying beside
you. Tell the person if you are not able to host a group or sustain
a long conversation. Care should take your present strength into
account.
Practical help can accompany the prayer. A ride, a meal, or help
with a recurring responsibility may answer a need you have
been trying to conceal. Be as clear as you can about what would
help and what you would prefer to do yourself.
A conversation with your medical team
Bring questions about your condition and treatment to the
people caring for you. If an explanation is unclear, ask for it in
ordinary words. You could ask what a treatment is meant to do,
which changes to report, and whom to contact if you are
worried.
Keep the instructions you have been given somewhere you can
find them. With your permission, a trusted person could help
you remember questions or attend an appointment. Their role
should support your understanding and choices.
Tell the team about the effect on your daily life as well as the
symptom itself. "I cannot stand long enough to prepare food"
may give a clearer account of a difficulty than simply saying you
feel weak. If distress or low mood is becoming hard to manage,
mention that too. Emotional care belongs alongside care for the
illness.
Receiving treatment does not prevent you from praying for
healing. Your prayer can include the judgment of clinicians,
relief from symptoms, and the people arranging care. Decisions
about medicines and treatment need appropriate medical
advice; a testimony about someone else's recovery cannot make
those decisions for you.

260
Strength when you have little to give
My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my
heart and my portion forever.
Psalm 73:26, Berean Standard Bible
Psalm 73 moves through troubled comparisons toward renewed
confidence in God's presence. Its speaker can acknowledge
failing strength while continuing to desire God. You can borrow
that language when your own strength is difficult to rely on.
Perhaps you have measured a faithful day by how much you
accomplish. Illness can expose how heavy that expectation has
become. Let someone read to you, shorten a prayer, or leave a
task for another day where it can wait. You remain a person to
be loved on a day when you need extensive help.
If someone you care about is ill
Ask before visiting and find out what kind of contact is welcome.
A person may appreciate a short conversation while finding an
unexpected afternoon visit exhausting. Follow any precautions
their medical team has advised.
Offer a specific task and respect a refusal. Avoid diagnosing the
illness, recommending a treatment from a story you heard, or
suggesting that stronger faith would secure recovery. Keep
asking about the person's interests as well as their condition.
Give prayer with their consent, and let it include their actual
concerns.

261
A prayer
Lord, I ask You for healing and relief. Give wisdom to those caring
for me and help me understand the decisions before me. Receive the
frustration of what I cannot do today. Provide the practical help I
need, and teach me to accept it with honesty. Be my strength in the
hours when illness occupies so much of my attention. In Jesus' name,
amen.
Pause and reflect
What part of being ill have you found hardest to explain?
Is there a question for your medical team or a practical request
you could make today?
For further reading: Mark 5:25–34; James 5:13–16; 1 Timothy 5:23; 2 Timothy 4:20;
Psalm 73:21–28; Psalm 41:1–3.
Read also:

attention.
• Living with Chronic Pain (p. 266), if pain has become an ongoing part of life.
• Caring for Someone Who Is Ill (p. 270), to share with someone helping you.
